summary.text: Writing each prime-power binomial step as a product over residues prime to \(p\), the proof pairs \(i\) with \(p^r-i\); reciprocal-square sum identities then control the product expansions, and their linear terms cancel using congruences for the preceding binomial coefficients. The exceptional cases use a sharper elementary-symmetric expansion when \(r=2\), while for \(p=3\) stable residues modulo \(3^5\), a weakened unit-sum valuation, and a direct finite base computation provide the missing powers of \(3\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\binom{3n}{n}^{2}-27\binom{2n}{n}.
\]
We prove that, for every prime \(p\ge 3\) and every \(r\ge2\),
\[
a(p^r)\equiv a(p^{r-1})\pmod {p^{3r+3}}.
\]

Throughout, congruences may be manipulated in the ring \(\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\). If an integer is relatively prime to \(N\), its inverse in that ring is denoted by the usual superscript \({}^{-1}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. The binomial step product
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For positive integers \(q\) and \(m\), the elementary product formula for a binomial coefficient is
\[
 \binom{(m+1)q}{q}=\prod_{i=1}^{q}\frac{mq+i}{i}.
\]
Suppose now that \(q=pn\), where \(p\ne0\). The factors indexed by multiples of \(p\), say \(i=pj\), have product
\[
 \prod_{j=1}^{n}\frac{mpn+pj}{pj}
 =\prod_{j=1}^{n}\frac{mn+j}{j}
 =\binom{(m+1)n}{n}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
 \frac{\binom{(m+1)q}{q}}{\binom{(m+1)n}{n}}
 =\prod_{\substack{1\le i\le q\\p\nmid i}}\frac{mq+i}{i}.
\tag{1}
\]
This identity can first be read over \(\mathbb Q\), and clearing the nonzero denominators gives an integer identity. Therefore, modulo any integer \(N\) for which every \(i\) occurring on the right is a unit, it becomes
\[
 \binom{(m+1)q}{q}
 =\binom{(m+1)n}{n}
 \prod_{\substack{1\le i\le q\\p\nmid i}}
 \left(1+mq i^{-1}\right).
\tag{2}
\]

We apply this with \(q=p^r\), \(n=p^{r-1}\), and \(N=p^{3r+3}\). The indices not divisible by \(p\) are precisely the unit representatives modulo \(q\). Write
\[
 \mathcal U_q=\{i:0\le i<q,\ (i,q)=1\}.
\]
(The set in (2) is the same set: neither \(0\) nor \(q\) is a unit.) Define
\[
 R_m=R_m(N,q):=\prod_{i\in\mathcal U_q}(1+mq i^{-1})
 \quad\text{in }\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z.
\tag{3}
\]
Then (2) says
\[
 \binom{(m+1)p^r}{p^r}
 =\binom{(m+1)p^{r-1}}{p^{r-1}}R_m.
\tag{4}
\]

The involution \(i\mapsto q-i\) permutes \(\mathcal U_q\). Multiplying the factor belonging to \(i\) by the factor belonging to \(q-i\), we obtain
\[
 (1+mq i^{-1})(1+mq(q-i)^{-1})
 =1+m(m+1)q^2\bigl(i(q-i)\bigr)^{-1}.
\tag{5}
\]
Indeed,
\[
 i^{-1}+(q-i)^{-1}=q\bigl(i(q-i)\bigr)^{-1},

after putting the two fractions over the common denominator \(i(q-i)\), and the quadratic term contributes \(m^2q^2(i(q-i))^{-1}\). Because replacing all indices by \(q-i\) leaves the product unchanged, (5) gives
\[
 R_m^2=
 \prod_{i\in\mathcal U_q}
 \left(1+m(m+1)q^2t_i\right),
 \qquad
 t_i:=\bigl(i(q-i)\bigr)^{-1}.
\tag{6}
\]
Set
\[
 T:=\sum_{i\in\mathcal U_q}t_i.
\tag{7}
\]
These quantities are always interpreted in the modulus currently under discussion.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Unit-square and reciprocal-sum facts
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We need several elementary sums over the units of a prime-power ring.

Suppose first that \(p\ge5\), and put \(Q=p^s\), \(s\ge1\). In \(\mathbb Z/Q\mathbb Z\), let
\[
 S_2=\sum_{x\in(\mathbb Z/Q\mathbb Z)^\times}x^2.
\]
Multiplication by \(2\) permutes the units, so \(S_2=4S_2\). Hence \(3S_2=0\). Since \(3\) is a unit modulo \(Q\), it follows that
\[
 S_2=0\pmod Q.
\tag{8}
\]
Inversion also permutes the units, and therefore
\[
 \sum_{x\in(\mathbb Z/Q\mathbb Z)^\times}x^{-2}=0\pmod Q.
\tag{9}
\]

For \(q=p^r\), reduction of the paired reciprocal gives
\[
 t_i=\bigl(i(q-i)\bigr)^{-1}\equiv(-i^2)^{-1}=-i^{-2}\pmod q.
\]
The representatives \(i\in\mathcal U_q\) run through all units modulo \(q\), so (9) yields
\[
 T\equiv0\pmod q\qquad(p\ge5).
\tag{10}
\]

We will also use the ordinary reciprocal sum modulo \(q^2\). Pairing \(i\) with \(q-i\), one has in \(\mathbb Z/q^2\mathbb Z\)
\[
 i^{-1}+(q-i)^{-1}=-q i^{-2}.
\tag{11}
\]
One way to see this is to note that
\[
 (q-i)^{-1}=-i^{-1}-qi^{-2}\pmod{q^2},

the right side becoming an inverse of \(q-i\) after multiplication. Summing (11) over all unit representatives and using that the involution preserves the sum gives
\[
 2\sum_{i\in\mathcal U_q}i^{-1}
 =-q\sum_{i\in\mathcal U_q}i^{-2}\pmod{q^2}.
\]
The inverse-square sum is \(0\pmod q\) by (9), and \(2\) is a unit because \(p\) is odd. Thus
\[
 \sum_{i\in\mathcal U_q}i^{-1}=0\pmod{q^2}
 \qquad(p\ge5).
\tag{12}
\]
Expanding (3) modulo \(q^2\), all terms of degree at least two contain \(q^2\), and hence
\[
 R_m\equiv1+mq\sum_i i^{-1}\equiv1\pmod{q^2}.
\tag{13}
\]

There is also a version of the last conclusion sufficient for \(p=3\), without using (12). In \(\mathbb Z/q^2\mathbb Z\), equation (6) has every factor equal to \(1\), since \(q^2=0\); hence
\[
 R_m^2=1\pmod{q^2}.
\]
On the other hand every factor in (3) is \(1\pmod q\), so \(R_m\equiv1\pmod q\). Write \(R_m=1+z\), with \(q\mid z\). Then \(z^2=0\pmod{q^2}\), and
\[
 0=R_m^2-1=2z+z^2=2z\pmod{q^2}.
\]
As \(2\) is invertible for every odd \(p\), this proves
\[
 R_m\equiv1\pmod{q^2}
 \qquad\text{for every odd prime }p.
\tag{14}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Linearizing the paired product when \(r\ge3\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Return to the modulus
\[
 M=p^{3r+3},\qquad q=p^r.
\]
If \(r\ge3\), then \(q^4=p^{4r}\) is divisible by \(M\), because \(4r\ge3r+3\). Therefore all products of two or more of the nonconstant terms in (6) vanish modulo \(M\). We consequently have the exact congruence
\[
 R_m^2-1=m(m+1)q^2T\pmod M.
\tag{15}
\]

Moreover, by (13) for \(p\ge5\), and by (14) for \(p=3\), \(R_m-1\) is divisible by \(q^2\). Since \(r\ge3\), its square is divisible by \(q^4\), hence by \(M\). Thus
\[
 (R_m-1)^2=0\pmod M.
\tag{16}
\]
Using
\[
 R_m^2-1=2(R_m-1)+(R_m-1)^2

a nd the invertibility of \(2\), equations (15) and (16) give
\[
 R_m-1=\frac{m(m+1)}2q^2T\pmod M.
\tag{17}
\]
In particular, if
\[
 U:=R_2,\qquad V:=R_1,
\]
then
\[
 U^2-1=6q^2T,
 \qquad
 V-1=q^2T
 \pmod M.
\tag{18}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. The coefficient congruence for \(p\ge5\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We next prove, for every \(s\ge0\),
\[
 \binom{2p^s}{p^s}\equiv2\pmod{p^3},
 \qquad
 \binom{3p^s}{p^s}\equiv3\pmod{p^3}
 \qquad(p\ge5).
\tag{19}
\]

First, Lucas's congruence modulo \(p\), applied successively to the trailing zero base-\(p\) digits, gives
\[
 \binom{2p^s}{p^s}\equiv2\pmod p,
 \qquad
 \binom{3p^s}{p^s}\equiv3\pmod p.
\tag{20}
\]
For the stronger statement, use the step product (4), now modulo \(p^3\). Its ratio is \(R_m(p^3,p^j)\). By (6), its square is the paired product. If \(j\ge2\), each nonconstant paired term contains \(p^{2j}\), hence vanishes modulo \(p^3\). If \(j=1\), expansion of the paired product leaves only
\[
 p^2m(m+1)\sum_{i\in\mathcal U_p}t_i;

after reduction modulo \(p\), \(t_i\equiv-i^{-2}\), and its sum is zero by (9). Thus in all cases
\[
 R_m(p^3,p^j)^2=1\pmod{p^3}.
\]
Induction from \(s=0\), using (4), shows that the squares of the two binomial coefficients in (19) are respectively \(4\) and \(9\) modulo \(p^3\). Together with (20), this selects the positive roots. Explicitly, if \(x^2=a^2\pmod{p^3}\) and \(x\equiv a\pmod p\), where \(a=2\) or \(3\), then
\[
 (x-a)(x+a)=0\pmod{p^3}.
\]
The factor \(x+a\) is nonzero modulo \(p\), because it is congruent to \(2a\), and \(p\ge5\); hence it is a unit modulo \(p^3\), forcing \(x=a\). This proves (19).

Let
\[
 n=p^{r-1},\qquad
 A=\binom{3n}{n},\qquad B=\binom{2n}{n}.
\]
By (19), \(A\equiv3\) and \(B\equiv2\pmod{p^3}\). Hence
\[
 C:=6A^2-27B\equiv6\cdot9-27\cdot2=0\pmod{p^3}.
\tag{21}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Completion for \(p\ge5\), \(r\ge3\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Let
\[
 A_q=\binom{3q}{q},\qquad B_q=\binom{2q}{q},
 \qquad q=p^r,

a nd retain \(A,B\) from the preceding section. Formula (4) gives
\[
 A_q=AU,
 \qquad B_q=BV.
\tag{22}
\]
By (10), \(T\) is divisible by \(q=p^r\). Thus (21) and the explicit factor \(q^2=p^{2r}\) imply
\[
 (6A^2-27B)q^2T\equiv0\pmod{p^{3+2r+r}}
 =0\pmod{p^{3r+3}}.
\tag{23}
\]
Using (18), (22), and (23), we calculate modulo \(M=p^{3r+3}\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
 A_q^2-A^2
 &=A^2(U^2-1)\\
 &=6A^2q^2T\\
 &=27Bq^2T\\
 &=27B(V-1)\\
 &=27(B_q-B).
\end{aligned}
\tag{24}
\]
Rearranging (24) is exactly
\[
 A_q^2-27B_q\equiv A^2-27B\pmod M,
\]
which proves the desired result in this case.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. The special case \(p\ge5\), \(r=2\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Here \(q=p^2\) and \(M=p^9\). The simple linearization used above is not automatic, because \(q^4=p^8\) need not vanish modulo \(p^9\). We therefore retain the quadratic term and show that it cancels.

Put
\[
 t_i=\bigl(i(p^2-i)\bigr)^{-1}\pmod{p^9},
 \qquad
 E_2=\sum_{\{i,j\}\subset\mathcal U_{p^2}}t_it_j.
\]
For any scalar \(c\) with \(c^3=0\), finite product expansion gives
\[
 \prod_i(1+ct_i)=1+c\sum_i t_i+c^2E_2.
\tag{25}
\]
In our situation \(c=Aq^2\), and \(c^3\) contains \(p^{12}\), so it is zero modulo \(p^9\).

We claim that
\[
 E_2\equiv0\pmod p.
\tag{26}
\]
Modulo \(p\),
\[
 t_i\equiv-i^{-2},

a quantity depending only on \(i\bmod p\). Every unit residue modulo \(p\) has exactly \(p\) unit lifts modulo \(p^2\), namely \(a+kp\), \(0\le k<p\). Therefore both
\[
 \sum_{i\in\mathcal U_{p^2}}t_i
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \sum_{i\in\mathcal U_{p^2}}t_i^2

a re zero modulo \(p\): each sum is \(p\) times a sum over the units modulo \(p\). Finally,
\[
 2E_2=\left(\sum_i t_i\right)^2-\sum_i t_i^2.
\]
Since \(2\) is a unit modulo \(p\), (26) follows.

Applying (25) to (6), with \(c=m(m+1)q^2\), the quadratic term is a multiple of
\[
 q^4E_2=p^8E_2,

a nd this is zero modulo \(p^9\) by (26). Thus the desired linearization remains valid:
\[
 R_m^2-1=m(m+1)q^2T\pmod{p^9}.
\tag{27}
\]
In particular, \(U=R_2\) satisfies \(U^2-1=6q^2T\).

For \(V=R_1\), we must again pass from its square to \(V-1\). We know from (13) that \(V\equiv1\pmod{q^2}=\pmod{p^4}\). Also (10) says \(T\equiv0\pmod{p^2}\). Reducing (27) modulo \(p^5\) therefore gives \(V^2-1=0\pmod{p^5}\), while \((V-1)^2=0\pmod{p^5}\) because \(p^4\mid V-1\). Hence
\[
 V-1=\frac12(V^2-1)=0\pmod{p^5}.
\]
It follows that \((V-1)^2=0\pmod{p^9}\). Using (27) once more in modulus \(p^9\),
\[
 V-1=\frac12(V^2-1)=q^2T\pmod{p^9}.
\tag{28}
\]
Thus (18) holds also when \(r=2\).

The coefficient \(C=6A^2-27B\) is divisible by \(p^3\) by (21), while \(q^2=p^4\) and \(T\) is divisible by \(p^2\). Their product is therefore divisible by \(p^9\). The calculation (24) now applies verbatim and proves the result for \(p\ge5,r=2\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. The necessary \(3\)-adic facts
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Now let \(p=3\), \(r\ge3\), \(q=3^r\), and \(M=3^{3r+3}\). Equations (15), (16), and (17) remain valid because the proof of (14) works for every odd prime. Thus (18) remains true. What changes are the divisibilities of the coefficient and of \(T\).

First we establish the coefficient congruence. For every \(s\ge1\),
\[
 \binom{2\cdot3^s}{3^s}\equiv20\pmod{3^5},
 \qquad
 \binom{3\cdot3^s}{3^s}\equiv84\pmod{3^5}.
\tag{29}
\]
For \(s=1,2,3,4\), these are direct finite modular computations from the binomial products; in each of these four cases the respective residues modulo \(243\) are \(20\) and \(84\). For \(s\ge5\), apply the step formula (4) modulo \(3^5\). Every factor in \(R_m(3^5,3^s)\) is
\[
 1+m3^s i^{-1}=1
 \pmod{3^5},

a nd hence the binomial coefficient at level \(s\) has the same residue as at level \(s-1\). Induction from the four initial cases proves (29) for all \(s\ge1\).

Taking \(s=r-1\), which is positive, gives
\[
 A=\binom{3\cdot3^{r-1}}{3^{r-1}}\equiv84,
 \qquad
 B=\binom{2\cdot3^{r-1}}{3^{r-1}}\equiv20
 \pmod{3^5}.

a nd a direct reduction modulo \(243\) gives
\[
 6\cdot84^2-27\cdot20\equiv0\pmod{243}.

a ccordingly,
\[
 C=6A^2-27B\equiv0\pmod{3^5}.
\tag{30}
\]

We next prove
\[
 T\equiv0\pmod{3^{r-1}}.
\tag{31}
\]
Let \(d=3^{r-1}\). Reducing a summand of \(T\) modulo \(d\), and writing \(a=i\bmod d\), gives
\[
 \bigl(i(3^r-i)\bigr)^{-1}
 \equiv(-a^2)^{-1}=-a^{-2}\pmod d.
\tag{32}
\]
Every unit \(a\bmod d\) has exactly three unit lifts modulo \(3^r\), namely
\[
 a,
 \quad a+d,
 \quad a+2d.
\]
Therefore, by (32),
\[
 T\equiv-3\sum_{a\in(\mathbb Z/d\mathbb Z)^\times}a^{-2}\pmod d.
\tag{33}
\]
It remains to show that the right side is zero. Let
\[
 S=\sum_{a\in(\mathbb Z/d\mathbb Z)^\times}a^2.
\]
Multiplication by \(2\) permutes the units, so \(S=4S\), whence \(3S=0\pmod d\). Inversion permutes the units as well, so
\[
 3\sum a^{-2}=0\pmod d.
\]
Together with (33), this proves (31).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
8. Completion for \(p=3\), \(r\ge3\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

As before, set
\[
 A_q=\binom{3q}{q},\quad B_q=\binom{2q}{q},
 \quad A=\binom{3\cdot3^{r-1}}{3^{r-1}},
 \quad B=\binom{2\cdot3^{r-1}}{3^{r-1}}.
\]
The step products give \(A_q=AU\) and \(B_q=BV\), and (18) gives
\[
 U^2-1=6q^2T,
 \qquad V-1=q^2T.

a lso, by (30), \(3^5\mid 6A^2-27B\), and by (31), \(3^{r-1}\mid T\). Since \(q^2=3^{2r}\),
\[
 (6A^2-27B)q^2T

a is divisible by
\[
 3^{5+2r+(r-1)}=3^{3r+4},

a nd therefore certainly by \(3^{3r+3}\). The same calculation as in (24) yields
\[
 A_q^2-A^2=27(B_q-B)\pmod{3^{3r+3}},

a nd hence the required congruence for \(a\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
9. The remaining finite case \(p=3,r=2\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Only one case is not covered by the preceding arguments. Here the modulus is
\[
 3^{3\cdot2+3}=3^9=19683.
\]
Direct evaluation gives
\[
 a(9)=\binom{27}{9}^2-27\binom{18}{9}=21966327267885,
\]
while
\[
 a(3)=\binom{9}{3}^2-27\binom{6}{3}=6516.
\]
Thus
\[
 a(9)-a(3)=21966327261369
 =19683\cdot1116005043,

a nd so \(a(9)\equiv a(3)\pmod{3^9}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
10. Exhaustion of cases
--------------------------------------------------------------------

A prime \(p\ge3\) is either \(3\) or at least \(5\), since \(4\) is not prime. Also an integer \(r\ge2\) is either \(2\) or at least \(3\). The four possibilities have been proved above:

* \(p\ge5,r\ge3\), in Section 5;
* \(p\ge5,r=2\), in Section 6;
* \(p=3,r\ge3\), in Section 8;
* \(p=3,r=2\), in Section 9.

Therefore, for every prime \(p\ge3\) and every integer \(r\ge2\),
\[
\boxed{\ a(p^r)\equiv a(p^{r-1})\pmod{p^{3r+3}}\ }.
\]
